 Versione italiana For many VAT-registered individuals , November is when a significant proportion of their tax and social security obligations fall due. In addition to advance tax payments , depending on the nature of the business, there are social security contributions and the usual operating costs . The challenge lies in balancing tax and social security contributions with the financial needs of the business.
After all, turnover does not necessarily correspond to available cash flow. An expected payment may arrive after the deadline for a tax payment, creating a temporary imbalance between income and expenditure.
 November advance payments and financial resources 
 30 November 2026 is a key deadline for many taxpayers: by this date, the second or single IRPEF advance payment must be made and, for VAT-registered businesses under the flat-rate scheme, the substitute tax* .
Under the historical method , advance payments are calculated on the basis of the previous year’s tax liability. Alternatively, the forecast method may be used, which allows for a lower expected tax liability to be taken into account; however, this option requires careful assessment: an insufficient payment may result in penalties and interest.
Knowing the amounts due in advance allows you to plan your outgoings and assess the resources available. Even a business current account can facilitate the monitoring of receipts and payments , particularly when you wish to keep business transactions separate from personal ones.
It is advisable, however, to distinguish between the bank balance and the sums actually available for use. A portion of the available funds may already be earmarked for taxes, contributions or other commitments.
 Social security contributions: different obligations and deadlines 
For craftsmen and traders registered with the INPS schemes, 16 November 2026 is the deadline for the third instalment of fixed contributions calculated on the minimum income threshold. Any contributions on the excess amount, however, follow the deadlines set for income tax**.
The situation differs for professionals registered with the INPS Separate Scheme and for those affiliated to an independent pension fund. 
There is therefore no single contribution schedule that applies to all VAT-registered individuals, and those who have to make multiple payments within the same month should consider the overall impact. A tradesperson, for example, may have to pay their contribution instalment in mid-November and meet other tax obligations at the end of the month, whilst the business’s regular outgoings continue.
 Cash flow and payment planning 
 Cash flow management requires looking beyond the account balance. It is necessary to consider invoices yet to be collected, payments already scheduled and the expenses required to keep the business running.
Careful monitoring of receivables from customers can help distinguish between payments that are reasonably expected and those that are uncertain. On the expenditure side, however, it is useful to identify commitments that cannot be postponed and assess which expenses can be scheduled for a later date.
Regularly setting aside a portion of receipts for taxes and social security contributions allows you to spread the financial burden over time, avoiding the need to raise the entire sum just before deadlines.
The aim is not only to meet the November deadlines, but also to maintain sufficient liquidity for December and the first commitments of the following year. 
 Sources: 
 * Italian Revenue Agency, 2026 Tax Calendar, 30 November obligations relating to IRPEF advance payments and the substitute tax under the flat-rate scheme.
** INPS, F24 form for craftspeople and traders; Circular No. 14 of 9 February 2026, Craftspeople and traders: contributions for the year 2026.
